ab initio.et: Borrowed from Latin ab initiō (“from the beginning”).

s: a diminutive of the male given name Abraham, from Hebrew
Abiturient; a pupil / student who is taking, or who has taken and passed, the Abitur (roughly, high-school graduate)
Abiturient.et: Borrowed from Latin abituriēns, present participle of abituriō (“to want to leave”).

s: a male given name from Hebrew
Abia.et: Borrowed from Latin Abīa, from Ancient Greek Ἀβῑᾱ́ (Abīā́), from Hebrew אֲבִיָה (ʾĂḇiyyā́, “worshipper of Jah”)

s: final exams taken by pupils at the end of their secondary education in Germany and Finland to attain eligibility for all kinds of universities (allgemeine Hochschulreife).
Abitur.et: Attested since the 1890s. A shortening of Abiturium n, itself short for Latin exāmen abiturium—in formal German of the 19th century rather found as Abiturientenexamen—, from abituriō (“to wish to leave”), desiderative construction of abeō (“to leave, go off”).…

abirren.et: From ab- + irren. Probably a calque of Latin aberrō.

s: inside out (with the inside surface turned to be on the outside)
äbich.et: From Middle High German ebich, from Old High German abuh, from Proto-Germanic *abuhaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂époh₃kʷos. Cognate with English awk, Old Norse ǫfugr, ǫfigr, afigr (“turned backwards”) and Gothic 𐌹𐌱𐌿𐌺𐍃 (ibuks, “turned back”).

Abisolierzange.et: From abisolieren (“to strip, to skin”) + Zange (“pliers”).

s: to take abitur, to take school leaving examination
abiturieren.et: From New Latin abiturire + -ieren, derived from abiī (“leave”) + -turiō (desiderative suffix).
